aid: Built on abbagliare (to dazzle) with the noun ending -mento: the dazzling itself, a sudden glare that blinds for a moment.
The present participle of abbagliare (to dazzle): the dazzling light, which is why the high beam carries this name.
Picture oncoming high beams that leave a driver unable to see: abbagliare is to dazzle someone with strong light.
why: Only restates the gloss with a picture; no hook.

aid: The past participle of abbagliare (to dazzle): dazzled, blinded for a moment by a strong light.
From abbigliare (to dress), a loan from the French habiller: what a person is dressed in, clothing or gear.
From a- and bino (double, a pair, as in "binary"): two things joined together as a pair.
Built on abile (able), as in the English "enable": abilitare is to make someone able in law, so to qualify or entitle them.
From the Latin habitaculum, a small dwelling, related to "habitat" and "inhabit": the part of the vehicle where the people sit.
Not "abusively": abusivamente means without authorization or unlawfully, as in something done without the required permit.
From accendere (to switch on, to light): the switching on, and so the ignition of an engine.
From accertare, built on certo (certain), as in "ascertain": the act of making certain, a check or official verification.
Built on certo (certain), like the English "ascertain": accertare is to make certain of something, and accertarsi is to make sure.
Not "acceptance" in general: accettazione is the admissions or check-in desk, the place that accepts people as they arrive.
From the late Latin aciarium, built on acies (a sharp edge): the metal that takes an edge.
From accingersi, to gird oneself, as in the English "cinch": to get ready to do something, so to be about to do it.
From a- and coda (tail, queue): to get in line at the tail of someone else.
From a- and cogliere (to gather, to pick): to gather in, so to take in, hold or accept.
Sounds like "a corner": picture noticing something just around a corner. Accorgersi means to notice or realize.
why: The "a corner" sound hook is strained and does not connect to noticing.

aid: From accorgersi (to notice): the small measures a careful person thinks of in advance, precautions.
From accorto (alert, shrewd), the participle of accorgersi (to notice): the quality of being alert, care or caution.
From a- and costa (side, rib, as in "coast"): to bring alongside, so to pull over toward the edge.
Not "accuses": said of a person, accusa means shows or suffers from a symptom, as in accusa stanchezza, feels tired.
From acqua (water) and ragia (pine resin): a solvent distilled from resin, turpentine.
Built on adeguato (adequate): to make something adequate, so to adjust or adapt it to a need.
new: From the Latin adaequare (to make equal), the source of "adequate": adeguare is to make something match a need, to adjust or adapt it.
why: Direction reversed: adeguato is the participle of adeguare, not its base; both come from Latin adaequare.

aid: Not "adherence" to a rule: aderenza is the grip of the tires on the road, the way they stick to it, as in "adhesive".
From the Latin adhibere (to apply, to put to use): something put to a given use, designated for it.
From adoperare (to use), built on opera (work, as in "operate"): to put oneself to work, to do all one can.
Built on fatica (effort, weariness), like the English "fatigue": the state of being worn out.
From a- and fianco (side, like the English "flank"): to come up at someone's side.
From affidare, built on fede (faith), as in "fidelity": fare affidamento su means to put one's trust in, to rely on.
From a fine che, literally "to the end that": so that, in order that.
From the Latin affluxus, as in "affluent" and "flux": a flowing toward, the flow or supply of something.
Built on fretta (hurry, haste): affrettare is to hurry, and affrettato is hurried or rushed.
From a- and fronte (forehead, front): to face something head on, as in "confront".
Built on agevole (easy), from agio (ease), which shares its origin with the English "ease": to make easier.
From agevole (easy), from agio (ease), which shares its origin with the English "ease": easily, without effort.
Built on gancio (hook): to hook one thing onto another, to hitch or couple.
Built on gancio (hook): the hooking, or a part catching on something.
From a- and giorno (day): to bring something up to date, literally up to the present day.
From a- and giro (turn, circle, as in "gyrate"): to go around something.
From the Latin agere (to do, to drive), the root of the English "agent" and "act": to act, to work.
Built on aletta, a small ala (wing): the rows of thin fins on an engine that help it shed heat.
Picture wings (ali) spread wide and no engine: an aliante is a glider.
Not only "alimentation" or diet: in a vehicle alimentazione is the supply of fuel or power that feeds the engine.
Built on laccio (lace, cord), like the English "lace": to fasten or buckle.
From allacciare (to fasten), built on laccio (lace, cord): a connection or hookup.
Built on lago (lake): for water to cover an area as if it were a lake, to flood.
Built on largo, which means wide, not large: allargare is to widen, and allargamento is a widening.
Built on leggero (light in weight): to make lighter, to ease.
Built on lena (stamina, breath): to build up someone's stamina, to train.
Built on lento, which means slack as well as slow: to make slack, to loosen.
Related to the English "lodge": alloggiare is to lodge or stay, and alloggio is lodging.
Built on lontano (far): to move away, literally to make far.
From allora (then) and che: at the moment when, a formal word for quando.
From altri (others): belonging to other people, as in la sicurezza altrui, the safety of others.
new: An old form of altro (other) meaning of others: belonging to other people, as in la sicurezza altrui, the safety of others.
why: altrui is the old oblique form of altro (Latin alter), not a derivative of the plural altri.

aid: From a- and monte (mountain): what things pile up to, like the English "amount", which comes from the same root.
From ammortizzare (to deaden), like the English "amortize", with morto (dead) at its root: the parts that deaden the jolts.
From an-, short for anti-, and abbagliante (dazzling): the beam that does not dazzle, the low beam.
new: From an- (not, as in "anonymous") and abbagliante (dazzling): the beam that does not dazzle, the low beam.
why: an- is the Greek privative prefix meaning not, not a short form of anti-.

aid: From andare (to go): the way something goes, its pace or gait.
From the Latin anellus, a little ring, related to the English "annular": a ring.
Not quite "with animosity": animosamente means heatedly, with too much spirit, from animo (spirit, mind).
Not "anticipate" in the sense of expect: anticipare means to do something earlier, and in anticipo means ahead of time.
From anti- (against) and furto (theft, related to the English "furtive"): a device against theft.
From the Latin ante (before) and stare (to stand): standing in front of something.
From anzi (rather) and che: rather than, instead of.
why: Only restates the gloss; anzi glossed as rather adds nothing.

aid: Built on panno (cloth): a glass covered as if by a veil of cloth, fogged or misted up.
Related to the English "apparatus", from the Latin apparare (to prepare): a device or piece of equipment.
Not the body's "appendix": here appendice is something added on, a small trailer or attachment hung onto a vehicle.
From appoggiare (to lean on), built on poggio (a knoll, from the same Latin word as "podium"): a support or footing.
From the Latin apponere (to place on), as in the English "apposition": apporre is to affix, and apposto is affixed.
Not "opposite": apposito means made for the purpose, the proper one, from the Latin appositus (placed next to).
new: Not "opposite": apposito means made for the purpose, like the rare English "apposite", both from the Latin appositus; appositamente means specifically, on purpose.
why: Aid omits that the true English cognate apposite shares the meaning; the gloss is appositamente, not apposito.

aid: From a- and profitto (profit): to draw profit from something, to take advantage of it.
Not "approximate": approssimarsi means to draw near, from the Latin proximus (nearest), as in "proximity".
Not an "arc" of a circle here: arco is a span of time, as in nell'arco delle ventiquattro ore, over the whole day.
From the Latin agger (a heaped wall of earth): an embankment that holds a river in.
From a- and recare (to bring): to bring on, to cause, usually harm or trouble.
Not only "arrest" by the police: arrestare mainly means to stop, and arrestarsi is to come to a halt.
Built on rotolo (a roll): the device that rolls the belt back up.
Related to the English "articulated", as in an articulated bus: the points where parts of the body bend, the joints.
Built on artigiano (artisan): made by hand rather than in a factory.
From the Latin artus (joint, limb), related to "article" and "articulation": an arm or a leg.
From the Latin exsuctus (sucked out), as in "suction": with the moisture drawn out, dry.
From asino, from the Latin asinus (donkey), the source of the English "asinine".
Short for Azienda Sanitaria Locale, the local health authority.
Related to the English "asperity" (roughness): both come from the Latin asper, rough.
Related to the English "axis" and "axle": both go back to the Latin axis.
new: Related to the English "axis": asse comes from the Latin axis, the rod that a pair of wheels turns on, an axle.
why: English axle is from Old Norse, a Germanic cognate; it does not go back to Latin axis.

aid: Sounds like "a set": the assetto of a vehicle is how it is set on its wheels, its balance and trim.
From a- and sicuro (sure, secure): to make sure or to make secure, as in the English "assure" and "insure".
From assicurare (to make secure, from sicuro): insurance is what makes one secure, as in the English "assurance".
Not "assimilated" in the sense of absorbed: assimilato means treated the same as or counted as equal to, from simile (similar).
From a- and soggetto (subject): made subject to, as in the English "subjected".
From sole (sun, as in "solar"): an assolata road is one exposed to the full sun.
Not "assume": assumere here means to take in or ingest a substance, and it also means to hire.
Not "assumption": assunzione here means the taking of a substance, and it also means hiring.
Not "attacked": attaccato here means attached or fastened, and it looks like the English "attach" as well.
Not "attend": attendere means to wait or to wait for.
From a- and tenersi (to hold oneself): to hold to a rule or instruction, to comply with it.
From terra (earth, land, as in "terrain"): atterrare is to come down to earth, to land.
From attendere (to wait): the attesa is the wait itself.
Not "acts" here: in atti a the word means suited to, from the Latin aptus, the source of the English "apt".
From a and torno (a turn, as in the English "turn"): around.
From traverso (across), as in the English "traverse": to go across.
From traverso (across), as in the English "traverse": through or across.
Picture a workshop full of attrezzi (tools): attrezzato means equipped, and attrezzature is the equipment.
Not "attrition" as in losses: attrito means friction, the rubbing that the English word originally named.
Related to the English "actuate": attuare means to put into action, to carry out.
From the Latin auris (ear), as in the English "auricle": the piece worn in the ear.
Related to the English "auxiliary": both come from the Latin auxilium, help.
Not "artist" or "autistic": autista means a driver, especially one who drives for others, from auto.
From auto and articolato (jointed, as in "articulated"): a truck in two jointed parts.
From auto and caravan (travel trailer): a travel trailer that drives itself, a motorhome.
Not a car: autocarro, from auto and carro (wagon, cart), is a truck, a motor wagon for goods.
From auto- (self, as in "autograph") and certificare (to certify): to certify something oneself.
From auto and cisterna (tank, as in the English "cistern"): a tanker truck.
From auto and demolitore (demolisher, as in "demolition"): the yard that breaks up old cars.
From auto and lavaggio (washing, from lavare, as in "lavatory"): a car wash.
From auto and rimessa (a place where things are put away, from rimettere): a garage.
From auto and snodato (jointed, flexible, from s- and nodo, knot): a bus that bends at a joint.
From auto and spazzare (to sweep): a vehicle that sweeps the street.
From auto and treno (train): a truck pulling a trailer, like a short train on the road.
From auto and velox (Latin for fast, as in "velocity"): a speed camera.
From auto and vettura (carriage, from the Latin vehere, to carry, as in "vehicle"): a passenger car.
From a- and valersi (from valere, to be worth, as in "value"): to make use of something.
From a- and venire (to come): to come about, to happen, like the English "advent".
Not "advertise": avvertire means to warn someone, and also to notice or feel something.
From a- and via (way): to set something on its way, to start it.
From vicino (near, as in "vicinity"): to bring or come near.
Not "advise": avvisare means to notify or to warn.
From vista (sight, as in "vista"): to catch sight of something.
From a- and volgere (to turn, as in "revolve"): to wrap by turning something around.
From azione (action): to put into action, to operate.
From the French azote, the old name for nitrogen, built from Greek words meaning without life.
From zero: azzerare is to bring something back to zero.
From the Latin balneum (bath): having to do with sea bathing and beach resorts.
A diminutive of banca (bench): a narrow strip, like a little bench, running alongside the roadway.
From the Greek barys (heavy, as in "barometer") and centro: the center of weight.
From battere (to beat) and strada (road): the part of the tire that beats the road.
Related to the English "band": a benda is a strip of cloth, and bendare is to bandage.
Not "benzene": benzina is gasoline, though the two names come from the same source.
Related to the English "beverage": both come from the Latin bibere, to drink.
From the Latin binarius (in pairs, as in "binary"): a track is a pair of rails.
From bi- (two) and via (way): the point where one road becomes two.
From the Latin bulla (seal), the source of the papal "bull": a stamp, here the one showing a tax is paid.
A diminutive of bombola (gas cylinder, canister): a small pressurized can.
A diminutive of breccia (broken stone, the English geological word "breccia"): fine gravel.
Sounds like "brr": brividi are the shivers or chills.
Related to buco (hole): a buca is a hole in the ground, and on a road a pothole.
Related to the English "chase" and "catch": all come from the Latin captiare, to try to seize.
Not "cold": calda means hot or warm, from the Latin calidus, the source of the English "scald".
Related to the English "calorie": both come from the Latin calor, heat.
Picture a skullcap: calotta is the dome-shaped outer shell, here of a helmet.
From calza (stocking, sock) and calzare (to put on footwear): footwear in general.
From campo (field, as in "camp"): to camp in the open, or the place where one camps.
Sounds like "canteen", but a cantiere is a work site, where building or road work goes on.
why: "Canteen" sound hook is weak and unrelated to the meaning.

aid: Related to cantone (district, as in the Swiss "canton"): the worker assigned to look after one stretch of road.
An augmentative of capanna (hut, cabin): a big shed, a warehouse.
Not a convoy of travelers: caravan here means a travel trailer towed behind a vehicle.
Related to the English "carburetor": carburante is any fuel an engine burns.
Related to the English "incarcerate": both come from the Latin carcer, prison.
Related to the English "cargo" and "charge": all come from the Late Latin carricare, to load a cart.
From carreggiare (to cart), from carro (cart): the part of the road made for vehicles, once for carts.
A diminutive of carro (cart, as in "car"): a small cart or trailer.
From the Latin carrus (wagon), the source of the English "car".
From carro (wagon) and attrezzi (tools, equipment): a truck carrying towing gear.
From carrozza (carriage): carrozzato means fitted with a body.
A diminutive of carrozza (carriage): a small carriage, a wheelchair or baby carriage.
From carrozza (carriage): the body of a vehicle, the part a carriage-maker built.
Related to the English "cartel", which came from the Italian cartello (placard): a sign or board.
Sounds like "cask": picture a hard cask worn over the head.
Sounds like casa (house): a caserma houses soldiers, firefighters or police.
A diminutive of cassone (large box, from cassa, as in "case"): a street trash bin.
Not "casual": casuale means accidental or random, happening by chance (caso).
Related to the English "catadioptric": a device that both reflects and refracts light, a reflector.
Related to the English "chain" and "concatenate": all come from the Latin catena.
From cavalcare (to ride astride) and via (road): a road that straddles another road.
Diminutive of cavallo (horse): a little "horse" that holds something up, like an English "sawhorse".
From the Latin clavicula (little key), the same word that gave English "clavicle".
From the Latin capulum (rope), the same source as English "cable".
Diminutive of centrale: a small central unit, the box that controls the electronics.
From cerchio (circle, hoop) with the enlarging ending -one: the large hoop of the wheel.
From the Latin clavus (nail), which also gave English "clove", the spice shaped like a small nail.
From ciclo (cycle, as in bicycle) and motore (motor): a bicycle-sized vehicle with a small motor.
From ciclomotore (moped) with the ending -ista, as in "cyclist": a person riding a moped.
From ciclo (bicycle) and pedonale (for pedestrians): for bicycles and pedestrians together.
From the Arabic sifr (empty, zero), the same source as English "cipher" and "zero"; here it means a figure or an amount.
From cilindro (cylinder): the total volume of an engine's cylinders.
From cingolo (crawler track), from the Latin cingulum (belt): fitted with a belt of links in place of wheels.
Related to ciondolare (to dangle): something that hangs and swings, such as a charm.
Not "circle": circolare means to travel or be driven on the road, the way traffic "circulates" through a city.
Not "circulation" of blood or newspapers: circolazione means road traffic, the movement of vehicles.
Not a "cistern" in the ground: cisterna here means a tanker, a vehicle carrying liquid in a large tank.
From Klaxon, the brand name of an early American electric car horn.
From clima (climate): the device that sets the climate inside the car.
From the Latin colligere (to gather), the source of English "collect": to pick up or grasp.
Past participle of coinvolgere, built on the same Latin root as English "involve".
From con- and laudare (to praise, approve, as in "laudable"): the test after which something is formally approved.
Plural of colla (glue), related to English "collage", a picture made by gluing.
Not "colleague": collegare means to connect or link, built on legare (to tie, as in "ligament").
From collegare (to connect), built on legare (to tie, as in "ligament"): a connection.
From con- and the Latin locare (to place), the root of English "locate": to put something in position.
Diminutive of colonna (column): a small post or bollard.
Not "colored": as a noun, colorito means complexion, the color of a person's face.
Related to English "commensurate": built on misura (measure), it means to size one thing in proportion to another.
Subjunctive of comparire (to appear), which shares the Latin parere (to show oneself) with English "appear".
From comparire (to appear): the moment something shows up, its appearance or onset.
From the Latin complere (to fill up), the source of English "complete": to carry something through to its end.
From compiere (to complete, from the Latin complere): the completion of something, such as reaching an age.
Not "complex": complessivo means overall or total, everything taken together.
Not "complicated": as a noun, complesso means a whole made of joined parts, like an English building "complex".
Not "comport": comportare means to entail or bring with it, as an act brings a consequence.
Not only "comprehend": comprendere most often means to include or comprise, and only sometimes to understand.
Not "comprehended": compreso usually means included, and compreso tra means lying between two limits.
Not "common" here: as a noun, il comune is the municipality, the town and its government.
Not a "concession" stand: a concessionario is a dealer licensed by a maker to sell its products, such as a car dealership.
Not "conducted" as in led an orchestra: condotto is the participle of condurre, to drive a vehicle.
Not "conduce": condurre means to drive or lead a vehicle, and the driver is the conducente.
Not a train "conductor": the conducente is the driver of a vehicle, from condurre (to drive, to lead).
Not "conducive": conducibile means drivable, able to be driven, from condurre (to drive).
From con- and ficcare (to thrust in): driven in and stuck fast.
Not "confine" as in lock up: il confine is a border or boundary, like the "confines" of a place.
Not "confront": nei confronti di means toward or with regard to, and a confronto is a comparison.
From con- and sapere (to know): knowing something fully, being aware of it.
Related to English "consign": both mean to hand something over to someone.
Not "consequence": conseguire means to obtain or achieve, as in obtaining a license.
Not "consequence": conseguimento means the obtaining of something, from conseguire (to obtain).
Not "consensus": consenso here means consent or permission.
Not quite "consent": consentire means to allow or permit, and è consentito means it is permitted.
From the Latin consilium, the source of English "counsel": to advise or recommend.
From consigliare (to advise, related to English "counsel"): advisable, recommended.
From contare (to count) and chilometri (kilometers): the counter of kilometers traveled.
Not "contemplated" as thought about: in legal Italian contemplare means to provide for or cover, as a law covers a case.
From con- and tempo (time): nel contempo means at the same time.
Not "contemporary" as modern: contemporaneamente means at the same time, the older sense of "contemporary".
Not "contextually": contestualmente means at the same time, in the same act.
Built on distinguere (to distinguish): to mark something so that it can be told apart.
From contra- and fare (to make): made in imitation, from the same Latin origin as English "counterfeit".
From contra- and segno (sign, mark): to put an identifying mark on something.
From contra- and segno (sign, mark): a mark or badge that identifies something.
From contro (against) and sole (sun): facing into the sun.
Not "convenient": conveniente means advisable or worthwhile, the better thing to do.
Not "convenient": conviene means it is advisable, it is the better course.
Not "convention" as a meeting: convenzione means an agreement or pact.
Related to English "convoy": to channel things or carry them along together.
Picture a cord laid along the edge of the road: a cordolo is a raised strip, such as a curb.
From corredo (outfit, a full set of equipment): furnished with the necessary items or documents.
Not "corridors": corridori are runners or racers, from correre (to run).
Related to correre (to run) and corso (course): the strip in which a line of traffic runs.
Related to English "cortege": both name a procession of people moving together.
From corte (court): an open court enclosed by buildings, a courtyard.
From così (so) and detto (said): literally "so said", the same idea as the English "so-called".
From costringere, from the Latin constringere (to bind tightly), the source of the English "constrain" and "constrict": to force.
Not "constructive" in the sense of helpful: costruttivo here means having to do with how a thing is built, its design or structure.
Not a "constructor" of buildings: costruttore here is the manufacturer, the company that builds the vehicle or the device.
From croce (cross) and via (road): the place where roads cross.
From custodire (to guard), the same root as the English "custody" and "custodian": watched over, kept under guard.
From danno (harm), from the Latin damnum, the source of the English "damage": danneggiare means to cause damage.
From the Latin damnum (loss, harm), the source of the English "damage": a danno is damage or harm.
From danno (harm), from the Latin damnum, the source of the English "damage": dannoso means harmful.
Taken from the French décoller (to unstick): the decollo is the moment an aircraft comes unstuck from the ground.
From de- and the Latin curtus (shortened), the root of the English "curt": decurtare means to cut down or deduct.
Not "definitely": definitivamente means permanently, once and for all, like "definitive" in the sense of final.
Not "denunciation": a denuncia (also spelled denunzia) is a formal report to the police or a claim to an insurer.
The verb behind the English "detergent": detergere means to clean or wipe a surface.
Not only "to determine": determinare often means to cause or bring about, and its participle determinato often means a specific or certain one.
From the same Latin root as the English "detergent" (detergere, to wipe clean): detersivo is the everyday word for a cleaning product.
Not simply "with difficulty": difficilmente usually means unlikely or hardly, as in something that hardly ever happens.
The feminine of direttore, related to the English "direct": a ruota direttrice is the wheel that directs the vehicle, the steering wheel.
new: The feminine of direttore, related to the English "direct": a ruota direttrice is the wheel that steers the vehicle, not the steering wheel in the driver's hands.
why: Aid called the ruota direttrice 'the steering wheel', which in English is the volante; the direttrice is the steered road wheel.

aid: From dirigersi (to direct oneself), from the same Latin root as the English "direct": dirigendosi means heading toward.
From dirigere (to steer, to direct), the same root as the airship called a "dirigible", a balloon that can be steered.
From dis- (removing) and appannare (to fog up), itself from panno (cloth): to clear the mist from the glass.
From dis- (undoing) and carica (load): the place where a load is unloaded and left, a dump.
Not "disciplined" in the sense of well behaved: disciplinato said of traffic or a crossing means regulated by rules or signals.
Not "discreetly": discretamente usually means moderately or fairly, as in fairly good.
new: Not only "discreetly": discretamente often means moderately or fairly, as in fairly good.
why: The gloss includes 'discreetly', and discretamente does carry that sense, so a flat 'Not discreetly' misstates it.

aid: From dis- (undoing) and inserire (to insert, to switch in): to take a device out of operation.
From dis- (difference) and livello (level): a difference in height between two surfaces.
Not "dispose of": disporre means to arrange or to order, disporsi to place oneself, and disporre di to have available.
From disporre (to arrange): a dispositivo is something arranged to do a job, a device.
Not "disposition" as in temperament: disposizione means an arrangement, or a rule laid down; a disposizione means available.
Not "disposed" (inclined): disposto means placed, or ordered by a rule, from disporre (to arrange, to order).
From dis- (undoing) and sesto (proper order, as in rimettere in sesto): a road that has lost its proper shape.
From distare (to be distant), the verb behind the English "distant": a place that dista a certain amount is that far away.
Participle of distendere (to stretch out), related to the English "distend": lying stretched out.
Not a "distributor" of goods: distributore di carburante is a gas station, the place that dispenses fuel.
Not "diverse": diverso means different, other than the one named; before a plural noun, diversi means several.
From vietare (to forbid), from the Latin vetare, the root of the English "veto": a divieto is a ban.
From the Arabic diwan (office, register), the same word behind the English "divan" and the French "douane": customs.
From the Latin dorsum (back), the root of the English "dorsal": the back of something, such as the hand.
From the Latin dorsum (back), like dorso: a dosso is a hump, the back of a rise in the road.
From dotare (to endow), from the Latin dos (dowry), the root of the English "dowry" and "endow": provided with, equipped.
Participle of dovere; dovuto a means owed to, and so caused by, much like the English "due", from the same Latin debere.
From effetto (effect): effettuare means to put into effect, to carry out, like the rare English "effectuate".
Not "efficient": efficace means effective, producing the intended result, like the English "efficacious".
Not only "efficient": efficiente said of a vehicle or device means in good working order.
Not only "efficiency": efficienza said of a vehicle or device means good working order.
From the Latin ens, entis (a being), the root of the English "entity": an ente is a public body or authority.
Sounds like "entry", but entro means within, or no later than: a limit of time or distance not to be passed.
Related to the English "equate" through the Latin aequus (equal): equiparato means treated as equal to another thing.
Not "heroine": eroina here is heroin, the drug, although the same spelling also means a heroine.
From the same Latin root as the English "execute" (exsequi, to follow through to the end): to carry something out.
From esigere (to require), from Latin exigere, the root of the English "exigency", a pressing need.
Not "expose" in the sense of uncovering: esporre means to display or put on show, as in the English "exposition".
Not "estate": estate means summer, from Latin aestas; the English "aestivation", a summer dormancy, shares the root.
From estate (summer), Latin aestas; the English "aestival", of the summer, shares the root.
new: From the Latin aestivus (of summer), related to estate (summer); the English "aestival", of the summer, shares the root.
why: Estivo is not formed from estate in Italian; it is the learned form of Latin aestivus, itself derived from aestas.

aid: Not "eventual": eventuale means possible or any that may occur, something that might happen rather than something that will happen in the end.
Not "eventually": eventualmente means if need be or possibly, in case the situation arises.
Not "to give evidence": evidenziare means to highlight or make stand out, from evidente (clearly visible).
Not "fabric": fabbrica means factory; the English "fabricate", to make, shares the Latin root fabrica (workshop).
Not "facility" as a building: facilità means ease, from facile (easy).
Not related to a "faculty" of teachers: facoltativo means optional, left to a person's facoltà, the power to choose.
Not a university "faculty": here facoltà means an option or a right, the power to do something if one chooses.
Related to fante, an old word for a small child, from Latin infans; the English "infant" shares the root.
From Gothic fani (mud); the English "fen", a marshy land, comes from the same Germanic root.
From Pharos, the lighthouse of Alexandria: a faro is a lighthouse, so a car's fari are its lighthouses.
From Latin fascia (band); English keeps the word for a band of tissue in anatomy and for a trim board on a building.
From fascia (band): to wrap with a band, that is, to bandage.
Not "fastidious": fastidio means annoyance or discomfort; both words come from Latin fastidium (distaste).
Not "fastidious" (fussy): fastidioso means annoying, something that causes fastidio (annoyance).
From fatica (effort, weariness); the English "fatigue" shares the root.
Not "factory": fattoria means farm; the Italian for factory is fabbrica.
From Latin ferire (to strike); the English "interfere" contains the same root.
From ferrovia, literally "iron way" (ferro, iron, and via, way), the Italian for railway.
From fianco (side, flank): to run along the side of something.
The same word as the English "flank"; Italian often turns fl into fi, as in fiamma (flame).
From Latin feria (holiday), the same source as the English "fair", a market or show.
From filo (wire) and bus: a bus that draws its power from overhead wires.
Diminutive of finestra (window): a small window.
Diminutive of finestra (window): the small windows of a car.
Not "firm" (a company): firma means signature, from firmare (to confirm); the English "confirm" and "affirm" share the root.
Related to the English "fix", in its sense of fastening in place; both come from Latin figere, fixus.
From Latin figere (to drive in), like fissare: things packed in tightly, as in fitta nebbia (thick fog).
From Latin flumen (river), the root of the English "flume", a channel for water.
From Latin folium (leaf), the root of the English "foliage".
Not "fund": fondo means bottom or surface, from Latin fundus (bottom); the English "profound", deep to the bottom, shares the root.
From forare (to pierce, make a hole); the English "perforate" shares the root.
From Latin fornix (arch or vault), a word English still uses in anatomy.
Related to the English "furnish", in its sense of to supply or provide.
From fosco (dark, dim), Latin fuscus; the English "obfuscate", to darken or obscure, shares the root.
Freccia is an arrow, and the turn signal takes the same name because it points the way.
From Latin frenum (bridle), the strap that holds a horse back; the English "refrain", to hold back, shares the root.
Not "frequency": here frequenza means attendance at a course, from frequentare (to attend).
Not "friction" here: frizione is the clutch, the mechanism that connects the engine to the wheels by friction between plates.
From fronte (front): to stand face to face with something, to confront it.
From Latin fugere (to flee), the root of the English "fugitive" and "refuge".
From Latin fumus (smoke), the root of the English "fumes".
From Latin funis (rope); the English "funicular", a railway pulled by a cable, shares the root.
From fuori (outside) and strada (road): a vehicle made to go off the road.
From fuori (out) and uscita (exit): something coming out, such as a leak.
From furgone (van): vehicles with a closed box body like a van's.
From the French fourgon, a covered wagon.
why: Only the French source fourgon, a word an American learner does not know; no hook.

aid: From Latin furtum (theft); the English "furtive", done secretly like a thief, shares the root.
From Latin cavea (enclosure), the root of the English "cage".
Not "gallery": on the road a galleria is a tunnel.
From gara (a race or contest): to take part in a race.
Formed from gas and olio (oil), like the English trade term "gas oil" for diesel fuel.
Not "gesture": gestire means to manage or handle, from Latin gerere (to carry on, conduct).
From Latin iactare (to throw), the root of the English "jettison", to throw overboard.
From Latin glacies (ice), the root of the English "glacier".
Sounds like "jacket" when said aloud, and it means the same thing.
From Latin genu (knee), the root of the English "genuflect", to bend the knee.
From Latin iudex (judge), the root of the English "judicial".
From Latin iungere (to join), the root of the English "junction": to arrive is to join the place one was heading for.
From godere (to enjoy), Latin gaudere (to rejoice), which also gave the English "joy" through French.
From Latin cubitus (elbow), the root of the English "cubit", a length measured from the elbow.
Not "gum": gomma means rubber, and by extension a tire; both words come from Latin gummi.
new: Not "gum" here: gomma means rubber, and by extension a tire. Both words come from Latin gummi, and gomma da masticare is chewing gum.
why: gomma also means gum (gomma da masticare, gomma arabica), so a flat "Not gum" is wrong; limited to this context.

aid: From gomma (rubber, tire): fitted with rubber tires.
From gomma (rubber, tire): the set of tires on a vehicle and their condition.
From gomma (rubber) with the augmentative -one: a big rubber boat.
From Latin conflare (to blow up), built on flare (to blow), the root of the English "inflate".
The initials of gas di petrolio liquefatto, the Italian for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG).
Diminutive of grado (step), Latin gradus, the root of the English "grade" and "gradual".
Sounds like grande (big): picture big stones of ice falling from the sky.
From grave (heavy), Latin gravis, the root of the English "gravity": to weigh down on something.
From the same Germanic source as the French gant, which gave the English "gauntlet".
Augmentative of guanto (glove), from the same source as the English "gauntlet": big, heavy gloves.
From guastare (to spoil), Latin vastare; the English "waste" and "devastate" share the root.
From the Latin idoneus (fit, suitable), which survives in the rare English word "idoneous": fit or qualified for a purpose.
From the Latin ignis (fire, as in "ignite") and fugare (to drive away, as in "fugitive"): a material that keeps fire away.
From barca (boat), the root also seen in the English "embark": any craft that carries people or goods on water.
Related to the English "embark": from in- and barca (boat), the act of going or loading on board.
From in- and bocca (mouth): to go into the mouth of a road, street or tunnel.
From matricola (an official register), as in the English "matriculate": to enter a vehicle in the official register.
From in- (into) and mettere (to put, from the same Latin root as "emit" and "admit"): to put oneself into a flow of traffic.
From immettere, in- (into) plus mettere (to put): the act of entering a road. The English "admission" comes from the same Latin root.
From pantano (a bog or swamp): stuck as if sunk in a bog.
From pegno (a pledge): to commit something, and on the road to commit the vehicle to a space such as an intersection.
From impegnare (to commit, from pegno, a pledge): something that demands a great deal of commitment or effort.
From in- and piantare (to plant, as in "implant"): something set firmly in place, such as a braking or electrical system.
Related to the English "employ", which came through French from the same Latin implicare: to put something to use.
Not "imports": importo means an amount of money, from importare in its sense of to amount to.
Not "impose" or "impostor": impostare means to set up or program something, such as a device or a route.
Not "imposition": impostazione is a setting, the way something is set up, from impostare (to set up).
From in- (not), pre- (before) and vedere (to see): not able to be seen in advance, like the English "unforeseeable".
From in- (not) and previsto (foreseen, from pre- and vedere, to see): events that nobody foresaw.
Not "improvised": improvviso means sudden, from the Latin improvisus (unforeseen), the same root as the English "improvise".
Not "impugned": impugnare here means to grip, from pugno (fist), the root also seen in the English "pugnacious".
From cammino (a path or walk, related to camminare, to walk): to set off walking.
From canale (channel, canal): to guide vehicles into a channel, as water is guided into a canal.
Not "incident" or "incise": incidere here means to have an effect on something, to weigh on it.
Not a minor "incident": incidente in Italian usually means an accident or crash.
From in circa, the same Latin circa used in English for approximate dates: all'incirca means roughly or about.
From colonna (column): to form a column, one vehicle behind another.
From the Latin incolumis (unharmed): the state of being safe from harm.
why: Latin incolumis gives an American no English link; the aid restates the gloss.

aid: Not "incumbent" in the sense of an officeholder: incombente means looming or impending, something about to fall on someone.
From croce (cross): to cross paths with another vehicle, including one coming the other way.
Not "indifferently": indifferentemente means either way, with no difference between the options.
Not "individualize": individuare means to pick out or locate, to single one thing out from others.
Not "individuation": individuazione is the act of picking out or locating something.
From in- and dosso (back, from the Latin dorsum, as in "dorsal"): to put clothing on one's back.
From the Latin indumentum (garment), from induere (to put on): the clothes a person wears.
why: Latin indumentum and induere give no English hook; the aid restates the gloss.

aid: Not "unfortunate": infortunato means injured, from infortunio (an accident that causes injury).
From fossa (a ditch or pit, as in the English "fosse"): sinking into a hollow, as a wheel does in snow or sand.
From in fuori (outward): all'infuori di means everything outside of, so except.
From gorgo (a whirlpool or eddy): a place where traffic swirls and stops, like water caught in an eddy.
Innestare is also the gardener's word for grafting one plant onto another; engaging a gear likewise fits one part into another.
From neve (snow): covered with snow.
From the Latin inquinare (to stain or defile): to pollute.
why: Latin inquinare gives no English hook; the aid restates the gloss.

aid: Related to the English "insufferable": insofferenza is the feeling of being unable to bear something, so impatience or annoyance.
Not only "integrated": integrare here means to complete or supplement, to add what is missing.
Not "integrative": integrativo means supplementary, adding to what is already there.
Not "interests": interessare here means to concern or affect, to involve a place or person.
From testa (head): a document intestato to someone carries that person's name at its head.
From intestare (to put in someone's name, from testa, head): the person whose name a document or vehicle is in.
From tralcio (a vine shoot): like vines tangled together, an intralcio is something that gets in the way.
Not "invalid" in the sense of not valid: invalido means a person with a disability.
From vecchio (old): the process of growing old.
Not just "inversion": inversione di marcia is a U-turn, reversing the direction of travel.
Not "invest": investire a person means to run into or run over them with a vehicle.
From the Greek hippos (horse, as in "hippopotamus") and dromos (course): a horse-racing track.
From rigido (stiff, rigid): to make or become stiff.
From lacrima (tear), as in the English "lachrymose": the flow of tears.
From lampo (a flash, as of lightning): lampeggiare is to flash on and off.
From lampo (a flash of lightning), which shares its root with the English "lamp": lampeggiare means to flash on and off.
From lampo (a flash of lightning), which shares its root with the English "lamp": a lampeggio is a flashing on and off.
Related to the English "launch" and "lance": lanciare means to throw or hurl.
Not "large": largo means wide, while the Italian word for large is grande.
Not "largeness": larghezza means width, from largo (wide).
From lavare (to wash, as in "lavatory") and cristallo (glass): the device that washes the windshield.
From lavare (to wash, as in "lavatory"): lavaggio is the act of washing.
From legare (to bind), the root of the English "ligament": a lega is an alloy, several metals bound into one.
From legare (to tie or bind), the same root as the English "ligament" and "obligate".
Not only a medical "lesion": lesione is the general word for a bodily injury, as in lesioni personali.
Not "lecture": lettura means reading, from leggere (to read).
Not an opera "libretto": here libretto means a small booklet, such as a vehicle's registration document.
From Latin levis (light), the root of the English "levity" and "alleviate": lieve means light or slight.
From Latin limitrophus (along the border), built on limes (boundary), as in "limit": limitrofo means bordering or adjacent.
Built on the same root as lungo and "long": a longherone is the long beam running the length of the frame.
From Latin macula (spot), the root of the English "immaculate" (spotless): a macchia is a stain or spot.
From maggiore (greater, as in "major") and -enne (years old, from anno): someone who has come of age.
Built like benessere (well-being) with male (badly) in place of bene: a feeling of being unwell.
From mano (hand) and mettere (to put): to put a hand on something, that is, to tamper with it.
From Latin manubrium (handle), itself from manus (hand): the handlebar is the part the hands hold.
From Latin manu tenere (to hold in the hand), the same root as the English "maintenance".
Not "marches": marce are the gears of a gearbox, as in cambiare marcia (to shift gears).
Not "march": marcia here means the movement of a vehicle, as in senso di marcia (direction of travel).
Made of marcia (going, walking) and piede (foot, as in "pedal"): the path for going on foot.
Not "march" on foot: marciare is said of vehicles and means to travel or drive along a road.
From mare (sea, as in "marine"): a storm at sea whose heavy waves strike the shore.
Originally a cooking pot, from the French marmite; the name passed to the car's muffler.
From maschera (mask): mascherare means to mask, that is, to hide or cover.
A diminutive of maschera (mask): a small mask or cover, such as the grille over a radiator.
Not "masses": massi are boulders or large rocks, as in caduta massi (falling rocks).
Not simply "maximal": a massimale is the maximum sum an insurance policy will pay, the coverage limit.
Related to the English "mastic", a resin used as a sealant: mastice is a sealing paste or glue.
From mediare (to mediate), built on medio (middle): mediante means by means of or through.
Not quite "medicate": medicare means to dress or treat a wound, for example with a bandage.
From Latin merx (goods), the root of the English "merchandise" and "commerce": merci are goods carried as freight.
From Latin misculare (to mix), the same root as "mesclun", a salad of mixed greens: mescolare means to mix.
From mezzo (middle, as in "mezzanine"): the mezzeria is the line down the middle of the road.
Not "mezzo" (half) as in mezzo-soprano: here mezzo means a vehicle, a means of transport, as in mezzi pubblici.
Related to the English "menace": minacciare means to threaten.
From minore (lesser, as in "minor") and -enne (years old, from anno): someone who has not yet come of age.
Molla means a spring; it comes from molle (soft, yielding), as in "mollify".
Related to the English "mole", a stone pier or breakwater: molo means a pier or dock.
From mono- (one, as in "monorail") and posto (seat): a vehicle with a single seat.
From the same root as "motor" and "locomotive": the motrice is the unit that moves and pulls the rest.
From mozzare (to cut off): a mozzicone is the stub left of something cut short, such as a cigarette butt.
From Latin munire (to fortify), the root of the English "munitions": munito means equipped or provided with.
A diminutive of muro (wall, as in "mural"): a muretto is a low wall.
From Latin nebula (mist, cloud), the root of the English "nebula" and "nebulous": nebbia means fog.
From neo- (new, as in "neonatal") and patentato (licensed, from patente): a driver who has just obtained the license.
Not "net" as in net weight: here netto means clean, clear or sharp, its original sense, from Latin nitidus (shining).
Not "noisy": noioso means boring or tedious; noia (boredom) shares its root with the English "annoy".
Built from non and che, literally "not that": nonché means as well as or and also.
From non and ostante (standing in the way, from Latin obstare, as in "obstacle"): with nothing in the way, that is, despite.
Not "notable" in the sense of famous: notevole means considerable, large in amount or degree.
Not "notably" in the sense of especially: notevolmente means considerably, to a large degree.
Not "occur": occorre means it is necessary or one needs. It shares the Latin root occurrere (to run toward), but in Italian it names what a situation calls for.
Not "occult" magic: occultare means to hide from view. Both come from the Latin occultus (hidden), as in an eclipse called an "occultation".
new: Not "occult" magic: occultare means to hide from view. Both come from the Latin occultus (hidden), since the occult was knowledge kept hidden.
why: An eclipse is not generally called an "occultation"; the astronomy hook was doubtful and obscure, replaced with the plain shared root.

aid: Not "office": an officina is a workshop, especially a repair shop for vehicles. The Latin officina already meant a workshop.
From oltre (beyond) and passare (to pass): to pass beyond a point or line.
Related to the English "homologation", used for racing cars: from the Greek homologein (to agree), it means officially certified as matching an approved type.
From opera (work), the root of the English "operate": an operaio is a manual worker.
Not "opera": opere is the plural of opera, a work; opere stradali are road works. The English "opera" comes from the same Latin word for work.
Not "opportunity": opportunamente means suitably, in the way the situation requires, like the rare English "opportune".
Not "opportunity": è opportuno means it is advisable, the right thing to do, like the rare English "opportune" (suitable).
Not body "organs" only: organi are also the working parts of a machine or vehicle.
Related to the English "ossify": both come from the Latin os, ossis (bone).
An old, formal form of dove (where), from the Latin ubi.
A diminutive of pala (shovel, blade): a paletta is a small paddle held up by hand.
Kept almost unchanged from the Latin palpebra (eyelid); doctors still use "palpebral" for anything about the eyelid.
From the Latin pannus (piece of cloth), the same word that gave the English "pane", once a strip of cloth.
From parare (to shield, as in parasol) and brezza (breeze): the glass that shields against the wind.
From the Latin par (equal), as in the English "par" and "parity".
From the Latin pascere (to feed, to graze), the root of the English "pasture" and "pastor".
From passeggiare (to go for a walk): a passeggino is the small wheeled seat for taking a child out.
Not only a "pastille" or lozenge: pastiglie are also brake pads, the small flat blocks pressed against the disc.
From pattino (a skate): a wheel that pattina slides as a skate does instead of gripping.
Same root as the English "pecuniary": the Latin pecunia (money), itself from pecus (cattle), when wealth was counted in livestock.
Sounds like "pedal": a pedivella is a lever moved by the foot.
Related to the English "pedestrian": both come from the Latin pes, pedis (foot).
From pendere (to hang, to lean), as in the English "pendulum" and "pending": the lean of a road.
The plural of pena, a penalty or punishment, as in the English "penal" and "penalty".
Related to pendere (to hang) and the English "pendulum": something penzolante swings loosely from one point.
From per (through) and correre (to run): to run through, to travel the length of a road. Percorso is the route covered.
Not "personal": as a noun, il personale means the staff, the English "personnel".
From per (for) and tanto (so much): for that reason, therefore.
From piano (flat, level), as in the English "plane" and "plain".
A diminutive of piazza: a small open space, here a paved area beside the road.
From piegare, from the Latin plicare (to fold), as in the English "pliable" and "ply".
From pietra (stone): a mass of small broken stones.
Not only the adjective "pneumatic": il pneumatico is a tire, a wheel cushion filled with air, from the Greek pneuma (air, breath).
From poggio (a rise, a support), from the Latin podium, as in the English "podium": poggiare means to rest one thing on another.
From poggiare (to rest on) and testa (head): the support the head rests against.
The source of the English insurance "policy", which came into English through French from this Italian word.
Related to the English "pulse": the wrist is where the pulse is taken, and both come from the Latin pulsus.
From the Latin pulvis, pulveris (dust), as in the English "pulverize".
From porre (to put, to place), from the Latin ponere, as in the English "position": ponendosi means placing itself.
From ponte (bridge): a walkway built out over the water, like a short bridge.
From porta (carries) and pacchi (packages): the rack that carries luggage on the roof.
From portare (to carry), as in the English "portable": what a vehicle is able to carry.
From porta (door): a portiera is the door of a vehicle.
Not "possibly" in the sense of perhaps: possibilmente means if possible, preferably.
Not the mail: here posta is the feminine form of posto, from porre (to place), so it means placed or located.
Built on posto (a place, a spot): posteggiare means to put a vehicle in its spot, the same as parcheggiare.
Built on pozza (a small pool of standing water), a relative of pozzo (a well).
From pre- (before) and avvisare (to warn, to notify): to give notice ahead of time.
From pre- (before) and avvisare (to warn), which shares its root with the English "advise": to warn ahead of time.
From pre- (before) and avviso (notice), which shares its root with the English "advice": a notice given ahead of time.
Not "precise": precisare is a verb meaning to specify or make clear, that is, to make something precise.
Not "precocious" in the sense of a gifted child: precoce means early or premature. Both words come from Latin praecox (ripened early).
Not "predispose" in the sense of being inclined: predisporsi means to get ready in advance, from pre- (before) and disporre (to arrange).
Not "predisposed" in the sense of inclined: predisposto means set up or arranged in advance for a purpose, from pre- (before) and disporre (to arrange).
Not "prejudice" in the sense of bias: pregiudicare means to harm or compromise, as in the legal English "to prejudice a case".
From Latin premere (to press), the root of the English "press", "pressure" and "compress".
From preporre (to put in front of or in charge of), the same root as the English "preposition": the person or office placed over a task.
Not a doctor's "prescription": prescrizione means a rule that requires or forbids something, from prescrivere (to lay down in writing).
From pre- (before) and segnalare (to signal): to signal something ahead of time.
From pre- (before) and segnalazione (signaling): a signal given ahead of time.
From Latin pressus (pressed close), the participle of premere: presso places something close by or at a place.
Prestare means to lend; prestare attenzione is to lend one's attention and prestare soccorso to lend aid, much as English says "lend a hand".
From prestare (to lend or provide): what a machine or a person provides, hence its performance.
Not "pretend": pretendere means to demand or to expect as a right, like the English "pretension" to a claim.
From pre- (before) and vedere (to see): to foresee. A law that prevede something has foreseen it, and so provides for it.
From prevedere (to foresee): something previsto has been foreseen, hence provided for or scheduled.
From principiare (to begin), related to principio (start): a principiante is someone at the start. The English "principle" shares the Latin root principium.
Privo di means lacking or without, related to the English "deprived" and "privation".
Not "procured" in the sense of obtained: procurare here means to cause or bring about, as in procurare un danno.
Not "projected": progettare means to design or plan, like drawing up a project.
Not "projected" in the sense of forecast: proiettare means to throw forward, as with the English "projectile".
Not a movie "projector": in a car the proiettore is the headlight unit, which throws light forward.
Not "proper": proprio means one's own, and as an adverb exactly or really. The English "proprietor" shares the idea of what is one's own.
From proseguire (to continue), which comes from Latin prosequi (to follow onward), the source of the English "pursue": a continuation.
Related to the English "pursue" and "prosecute": all come from Latin prosequi (to follow onward). Proseguire is to go on, to continue.
Related to the English "protracted": from Latin protrahere (to drag out). Something that si protrae drags on in time.
From pro- (forth) and venire (to come): to come forth from a place. The English "provenance" shares the root.
Not "provoke" as in making someone angry: provocare means to cause or bring about, as the English "provoke a reaction" does.
Not simply "provide": provvedere means to take the necessary steps or see to something. Both words come from Latin providere (to foresee).
From provvedere (to see to, supply): provvisto di means supplied or equipped with, close to the English "provided with".
Not "psychic" in the sense of reading minds: psichico means mental or psychological.
From Latin pulsare (to push or strike), related to the English "pulse" and "repulse": the pulsante is the thing one pushes.
Punta means a pointed tip, related to the English "point" and "puncture".
Built on punto (point): the total of points, a score.
A short form of pure (also, even): pur with a gerund means even while or even though.
Made of pur (only) and che (that): only on the condition that, provided that.
Quadro means a square frame or panel, from Latin quadrus (square); the quadro elettrico in a car is the instrument and ignition panel.
A quintale is a hundred kilograms; the word comes from the Arabic qintar, a unit of weight, and English has it as "quintal".
Built on doppio (double): to make double.
Built on figura (figure, picture): to show in a figure or picture.
Built on forza (strength, force): to make stronger, to reinforce.
Built on freddo (cold): making cold, hence cooling.
Built on freddo (cold): raffreddarsi is to become cold.
Raggio means a ray, and also the radius of a circle; both senses come from Latin radius.
Built on lento (slow): to make slower, to slow down.
Built on lento (slow): a slowing down.
Not "rapport" or "report": rapporto here means a ratio, or a relationship between two things.
new: Not "rapport": here rapporto means a ratio, or a relationship between two things. It can also mean a report, but not in these statements.
why: rapporto does also mean report, so the flat denial is wrong.

aid: Picture the spokes of a steering wheel radiating from the hub like rays; this razza is a spoke and has nothing to do with razza meaning breed.
Short for responsabilità civile auto: civil liability for motor vehicles.
Not "realized" in the sense of understood: realizzare means to make real, that is, to build or carry out.
From Latin reatus, built on reus (the accused person): a reato is an offense that makes someone a defendant.
From recare (to carry or bring): recante means bearing or carrying, as a sign bears a symbol.
From cingere (to encircle, gird), related to the English "cincture": recintare is to enclose with a fence, and a recinto is the enclosure.
Not only "regularly": regolarmente often means properly, in accordance with the rules.
Regolarsi is to regulate oneself: to adjust one's behavior to the situation.
Not "relative" as a family member or as "comparative": relativo means belonging to or corresponding to the thing just named.
Not "render" in the sense of drawing or paying: rendere usually means to make, as in rendere difficile, like the English "render useless".
From rendere (to give back, yield): what a machine gives back, its efficiency or output.
Related to the English "restitution": restituire means to give back.
From restringere (to narrow), the same Latin word that gave the English "restrict": a narrowing.
Not "retro" as in old-fashioned: retro means the back or rear, from Latin retro (backward).
From retro (backward) and cedere (to go, give way), related to the English "recede": to go backward.
From retro (backward) and marcia (gear, march): the backward gear.
Related to the English "rectilinear": from retto (straight) and linea (line), a straight stretch of road.
Not a "revision" of a text: revisione means an official inspection or re-examination, from rivedere (to look at again).
new: Not a "revision" of a text: revisione means an official inspection or re-examination, from the Latin revidere (to look at again).
why: Revisione is a Latinism from revisio/revidere, not a derivative of rivedere.

aid: Built on alzare (to raise), with ri-: raised up.
Picture a table flipped over: ribaltare is to tip over or overturn, and ribaltamento is the overturning.
From ri- (again) and chiamare (to call): to call back, or to call attention to something.
From ri- and chiedere (to ask): to ask for, hence to require.
From richiedere (to request): the person making a request, the applicant.
Not "recur": ricorrere a means to turn to or resort to someone or something, literally to run back to it (ri- and correre, to run).
From ri- (again) and fornire (to supply, the same root as the English "furnish"): supplying the vehicle again, that is, refueling.
The Italian ruler, righello, is named after riga: a riga is the straight line a ruler draws, and so a line or row of text.
From riga (line): a surface that is rigata has lines drawn across it, that is, it is scratched.
Not "release": rilasciare a document means to issue it, as an office issues a license or a certificate.
Not "release": rilascio is the issuing of a document, such as a license or a certificate, from rilasciare (to issue).
From rilevare (to detect or take a reading): rilevamento is the act of detecting or measuring something, as a sensor does.
From rimorchiare (to tow): the rimorchio is the vehicle that is towed, that is, a trailer.
Not "repair": riparo means shelter or protection, from riparare in its other sense of to shield someone from harm.
From ri- and partire (to leave): ripartire means to set off again. A second verb, built on parte (part), means to divide into parts, as a load is distributed.
Picture a high riverbank, ripa in Italian: a ripida road climbs as steeply as the face of that bank.
From ri- and piegare (to fold or bend), which comes from the Latin plicare, the root of the English "pliable".
Not "report" as in a news story: riportare here means to show or bear written text, as a sign bears place names. Both come from Latin reportare, to carry back.
From riporre (to put away or store), from ri- and porre (to put), the Latin root of the English "deposit": riposto means put away, stored.
From riprendere (to take up again): ripresa is starting up again. The English "reprise" comes from the same Latin verb through French.
From ri- and pristino (original, as in the English "pristine"): to bring something back to its original state, that is, to restore it.
From quadro (square or frame), related to the English "quadrant": a riquadro is a framed box within a sign or panel.
From ri- and salire (to go up): to go back up, and so to trace something back to its source, such as a plate back to its owner.
From the Latin resarcire, to patch or mend: risarcire means to make good a loss by paying for it, and risarcimento is that payment.
Built on scuotere (to shake): riscuotere means to collect money that is owed, as an insurer collects premiums.
From a Germanic root shared with the English "spare": risparmiare means to save or to spare, as in sparing fuel.
From ristretto (narrow or restricted), from the same Latin as the English "restricted": ristrettezza is narrowness.
Not "retain": ritenere means to believe or consider, as in ritengo che, I believe that.
Not "retirement": ritiro means a withdrawal or taking back, as when a license is taken away, from ritirare (to withdraw or collect).
From ri- (again) and vendere (to sell), as in the English "vendor": a rivenditore resells goods, that is, a dealer or retailer.
From ri- and volgere (to turn), the Latin root of the English "revolve": rivolgersi a means to turn to someone for help.
From rivolgere (to turn toward), the same Latin root as "revolve": rivolto means turned toward, directed at or addressed to.
From the Latin rota (wheel), as in the English "rotate": the rotaie are the rails that the wheels of a tram or train run on.
From rottame (scrap or wreckage), which comes from rotto (broken): to rottamare a vehicle is to turn it into scrap.
From rotto (broken), the past participle of rompere; the English "rupture" comes from the same Latin root.
Borrowed from French, from rouler (to roll): a small house on wheels that is towed, which Americans call a travel trailer.
From rovesciare (to overturn or spill), from the same Latin root as the English "reverse": turning something upside down.
From the Latin aerugo, the green rust that forms on copper: ruggine is the red-brown rust on iron.
From ruga (wrinkle), the root of the English "corrugated": a surface full of small ridges, that is, rough.
Not "rumor": rumore means noise, any sound, such as that of an engine or a horn.
Not "rumored": rumoroso means noisy, from rumore (noise).
Not about rumors: rumorosità is the noise level, from rumore (noise).
From ruota (wheel) with the small ending -ino: a little wheel, the narrow spare wheel carried for emergencies.
Sounds like "rude", and a ruvido surface is rude to the touch: rough and coarse.
Picture a cardboard cutout of a person: that flat outline is a sagoma, the shape or profile of an object.
From saldo (firm or solid), which comes from the Latin solidus, the root of the English "solid": firmly.
From saldare (to weld), which comes from saldo (solid). The English "solder" has the same Latin root.
From saltellare (to hop), a small form of saltare (to jump); the English "somersault" also goes back to the Latin saltus, a leap.
From salvare (to save) and gente (people): a thing that keeps people safe, here a raised island where pedestrians wait.
Like the old English "save" in "all save one": salvo means except or unless. Both come from the Latin salvus (safe).
From sangue (blood), the root of the English "sanguine": sanguinamento is bleeding.
Built on banda (side), an old word for the side of a ship: sbandare is to veer or skid to one side.
From s- and barra (bar), as in the English "bar" and "barrier": closed off by a bar.
Related to the English "bar": the sbarre are the bars that drop across the road at a crossing.
From s- (out of) and bocca (mouth): the place where one road comes out onto another.
From s- (removing) and brina (frost): to take the frost off, that is, to defrost.
From s- and cadere (to fall): a deadline falls due and passes, so scadere means to expire.
From scalzo (barefoot), built on calza (sock): scalzarsi is to come off the foot and leave it bare.
new: From scalzo (barefoot), from the Latin calceus (shoe): scalzarsi means to take off one's shoes, and scalzamenti are shoes slipping off the foot.
why: scalzo comes from Latin calceus (shoe), not from calza; and scalzarsi means a person takes off their shoes, not that a shoe comes off.

aid: From scaricare (to unload), from s- and carico (load): unloading, and the tubo di scarico that discharges the exhaust.
Picture the snap of a spring-loaded trap: scattare means to spring into action or be triggered, as a light switches on.
Sounds like the noise it describes: a schiaffo is a slap.
From schiena (back): the schienale is the part of a seat that supports the back.
From a Germanic root shared with the English "eschew": schivare means to avoid something by moving aside, to dodge.
Sounds like "ski" at its start: scivolare is to slide or slip, as a ski slides on snow.
new: Starts with sci, which is the Italian word for ski: scivolare is to slide or slip, as a ski slides on snow.
why: Italian sci is pronounced shee, so it does not sound like English ski; the true link is the spelling sci, the Italian word for ski.

aid: Sounds like "ski" at its start: scivoloso means slippery, a surface on which things slide as a ski slides on snow.
new: Starts with sci, which is the Italian word for ski: scivoloso means slippery, a surface on which things slide as a ski slides on snow.
why: Same sound-alike problem as scivolamento; the link is the Italian word sci.

aid: Not "scholar": scolaro means a schoolchild, a pupil, from scuola (school).
Related to the English "conjure": both come from the Latin coniurare, and scongiurare means to avert or ward off a danger.
Not "disconnection": sconnessioni are the broken, uneven patches of a road surface whose pieces no longer fit together.
From s- (not) and consigliare (to advise), from the same Latin as the English "counsel": advised against.
Not "scope": scopo means purpose or aim. The English "scope" comes from this Italian word, whose first meaning was a target to aim at.
Sounds like a burst or a pop: scoppiare means to burst or break out, and a motore a scoppio is a combustion engine.
From s- and correre (to run): to run along, that is, to flow.
From scorrere (to run along or flow), built on correre (to run): moving freely, and so sliding or free-flowing.
From scorrere (to run along or flow), built on correre (to run): a strada a scorrimento veloce is a road where traffic flows fast.
Sounds like a slip and a slither at once: sdrucciolevole means slippery.
why: The hook names no real sound-alike and only restates the gloss.

aid: Related to the English "see" in "the Holy See": both come from the Latin sedes (seat), and sede means a seat, office or site.
From sedere (to sit), as in the English "sedentary": the sedile is a seat.
From segare (to saw): segatura is the dust that sawing leaves behind, sawdust.
From seggiola (chair) with the small ending -ino: a little seat, the child seat.
From the Latin sella (seat), related to sedere (to sit): a saddle.
From the Latin silva (forest), as in the English "sylvan" and "savage": living wild.
From semi- (half) and carreggiata (roadway): one half of the roadway, the side used by one direction of traffic.
From semi- (half) and rimorchio (trailer): a semi-trailer, which has no front axle and rests its front on the tractor.
From se (itself) and movente (moving): moving by itself, that is, self-propelled.
Not "sensible": sensibile means noticeable or considerable, as in a change large enough to be sensed.
Not only "sense": senso often means direction, as in senso unico (one way) and senso di marcia (direction of travel).
From serbare (to keep, related to the English "conserve" and "reserve"): a container where something is kept.
From servire (to serve): servirsi di means to make something serve oneself, that is, to use it.
From servo (as in "servomechanism") and freno (brake): a brake whose force is boosted by a servo.
From servo (as in "servomechanism") and sterzo (steering): steering whose force is boosted by a servo.
From sfilare, s- (off) and filo (thread): to slide something off, the way a thread is drawn out.
From fiore (flower, and in older Italian the top surface of something): sfiorare is to touch only the surface, to graze.
new: From fiore in its sense of top surface, as in a fior d'acqua (at the surface of the water): sfiorare is to touch only the surface, to graze.
why: The surface sense of fiore is still current in set phrases, not only older Italian.

aid: From s- (out) and fondo (bottom): to knock the bottom out of something, to break through it.
From sfregare, built on fregare (to rub), which comes from Latin fricare, the root of the English "friction".
From frutto (fruit): sfruttare is to draw all the fruit out of something, to make full use of it or exploit it.
From s- (un-) and gancio (hook): sganciare is to unhook, to unhitch or unfasten.
The opposite of ingombrare (to obstruct, from the same root as the English "encumber"): sgombrare is to clear away, and sgombro means clear.
From sgombrare (to clear) and neve (snow): a machine that clears the snow, a snowplow.
The opposite of gonfiare (to inflate, blow up): the prefix s- undoes it, so sgonfiare is to deflate.
From s- (removing) and grasso (fat, grease, related to the English "grease"): to remove the grease, to degrease.
From sigillo (seal), the same Latin word that gives the English "sigil", a seal or sign.
From sintonia (being in tune), Greek syn (together) and tonos (tone): to bring the radio into the same tone as the station.
From slitta (sled): slittare is to slide the way a sled does, losing grip.
The opposite of montare (to mount, assemble): smontare is to take apart or remove, like the English "dismount".
Built on balzo (a leap, a bounce): sobbalzare is to give a sudden jump, to jolt.
From Latin succurrere (to run to help), the root of the English "succor": to come to the aid of someone.
From Latin sulcus (furrow), a word anatomists still use in English for a groove.
Not "solitarily": solitamente means usually, from solito (usual, customary).
Not "solicitously": sollecitamente means promptly, without delay.
Not "solicit": sollecitare means to urge or hurry someone, and said of a part or material, to put it under stress.
Not "solicitations": sollecitazioni are stresses or strains acting on a part or material.
From Latin sublevare, sub (from below) and levare (to lift), as in the English "lever" and "elevate": to lift up.
Related to the English "administer": both come from Latin ministrare (to serve, supply). Somministrare is to give a medicine or a drink.
Related to the English "somnolent" (sleepy): both come from Latin somnus (sleep), the root of sonno.
From sopra (over, beyond) and giungere (to arrive): to arrive on the scene, to come up from behind.
new: From sopra (over, beyond) and giungere (to arrive): to arrive on the scene, as a vehicle that comes up or approaches.
why: Sopraggiungere does not mean coming from behind specifically; oncoming vehicles also sopraggiungono.

aid: From sopra (over) and valutare (to value, evaluate): to overvalue, to overestimate.
From sordo (deaf) and cieco (blind): deaf and blind at once.
From Latin surgere (to rise), the root of the English "surge" and "resurgence": to rise or arise.
From sopra (over, beyond) and passare (to pass), like the English "surpass": to pass another vehicle.
From sostare, Latin substare (to stand still): a halt, here a vehicle left standing.
From sostenere (to hold up, related to the English "sustain"): a support or stand.
Not only "sustain": sostenere means to hold up or support, and sostenere un esame means to take an exam.
new: Not only "sustain": sostenere means to hold up or support, and a velocità sostenuta is a high speed.
why: The aid missed the gloss's high-speed sense and added an exam sense the bank does not use.

aid: From sotto (under) and passaggio (passage): a passage that runs underneath, an underpass.
From sotto (under) and porre (to put): sottoporsi is to put oneself under something, to undergo it, like the English "submit".
From sotto (below) and stante, from stare (to stand, be): standing or lying underneath.
From sotto (under) and stimare (to estimate): to estimate too low, to underestimate.
From sotto (under) and valutazione (evaluation): valuing something too low, underestimation.
From sotto (under) and via (way, road): a road that passes underneath, an underpass.
The Italian form of "subtraction", from Latin subtrahere (to draw away): a taking away or deduction.
From sovra (over) and carico (load): an overload.
From sovra (over) and numero (number): over the permitted number.
From sovra (over) and passaggio (passage): a passage that runs overhead, an overpass.
From Latin spargere (to scatter), the root of the English "sparse" and "disperse": to scatter or spill.
From spartire (to divide, share out) and traffico (traffic): the strip that divides the traffic, a median.
Related to paura (fear): both come from Latin pavere (to be afraid). Spaventare is to frighten.
From spazzare (to sweep): spazzatura is what is swept up, the garbage.
From Latin speculum (mirror), from specere (to look), as in the English "inspect".
A small specchio (mirror), from Latin speculum, from specere (to look), as in the English "inspect".
Not "species": specie, alone or in in specie, here means especially.
From spesso in its older sense, thick (the adverb "often" comes from the same word): how thick something is.
new: From spesso (thick), the same word that serves as the adverb often: spessore is how thick something is.
why: Spesso still means thick in current Italian; it is not an older sense.

aid: From Latin spectare (to look toward): spettare a means to be due to someone, to be their task.
Not only "spy": spia is also a warning light, the small eye on the dashboard that reports a fault.
From porgere (to hold out, hand over) with s- (out): sporgere is to stick out beyond an edge, and a sporgenza is what sticks out.
Picture a small porta (door): a sportello is a small door, such as a car door or a service window.
The opposite of provvisto (provided, from provvedere, related to "provide"): sprovvisto means lacking, not equipped with.
From s- (un-) and equilibrio (balance, "equilibrium"): thrown out of balance.
Not "establishment" in the sense of a shop or an elite: a stabilimento is a factory or plant.
From staccare (to detach) and batteria (battery): the switch that detaches the battery.
The opposite of attaccare (to attach): staccare is to detach.
Not "stall" as in an engine stalling: a stallo is a marked space where a vehicle stands, like a horse in its stall.
From stampa (print, related to the English "stamp"): marked with a stamp.
new: Related to stampa (print) and the English "stamp": stampigliare is to mark with a stamp.
why: Stampigliare comes from stampiglia, not directly from stampa; the claim is softened to a relation.

aid: Not a US state: statale refers to the Italian national state, so a strada statale is a national road.
Not "station" as a place: stazionare means to stand or stay parked in one place, from Latin stare (to stand).
Sounds like "steer": sterzare is to steer or swerve, and sterzo is the steering.
Sounds like "steer": sterzo is the steering, and a sterzata is a steering movement or swerve.
Not only "stipulate": stipulare is to conclude or sign a contract, such as an insurance policy.
Not "stranger": straniero means foreign or a foreigner.
Related to the English "stratum" (plural strata): a layer.
From stretto (narrow): a strettoia is a narrow spot where the road tightens.
Related to the English "stringent" and "constrict": all go back to the Latin stringere (to draw tight).
Sounds like "string": a stringa is the string that ties a shoe, a shoelace.
Picture a long narrow band of paint: a striscia is a stripe, and strisce are the lines painted on the road.
why: Picture restates the gloss and gives no hook.

aid: From strisciare (to drag or crawl along a surface): the sliding of a tire across the road.
Picture a snake: strisciare means to crawl or drag along the ground.
From the Latin subire, sub (under) and ire (to go): literally to under-go, exactly like the English "undergo".
Not "successfully": successivamente means afterward or later, from successivo (next).
Not "successful": successivo means next or following, like the English "successive".
Sounds like "sole": suolo is the ground, the surface the sole of a shoe rests on.
From the Latin superare (to go over), built on super (above): to get over a line, a limit or another vehicle.
From sur- (over, as in "surcharge") and riscaldare (to heat up, from caldo, hot): to heat too much.
From s- (un-) and viluppo (a tangle): to unwrap, the same picture as the English "develop", which first meant to unwrap.
From s- (un-) and vincolo (a tie or bond): the point where traffic is released from the main road.
From s- (out) and volgere (to turn, as in "revolve"): to unroll, and so to carry out or to take place, like the Latin root of "evolve".
Built on voltare (to turn), the root of the English "volte-face": svoltare is to turn off in a new direction.
