From s- and vuoto (empty): to make something empty.
From tale (such): taluni means certain ones, some but not all.
From tal(e) (such) and volta (time): at such times, so sometimes.
Related to the English "tambourine": a tamburo is a drum, and a drum brake takes its name from the shape.
From tampone (a plug, pad or buffer), related to the English "tampon": to press against something, and in traffic, to strike the vehicle in front.
Not "tangential" in the sense of off-topic: a tangenziale is a ring road or bypass, a road that touches the edge of a city like a tangent line.
Related to the English "tapestry": both go back to a Greek word for a rug or carpet.
Related to the English "tare", the weight of an empty container: tarare is to set or calibrate an instrument.
Related to the English "target", which first meant a small shield: a targa is the flat plate that carries a vehicle's registration.
Diminutive of targa (plate), related to the English "target", which first meant a small shield: a small identifying plate or tag.
From tela (cloth): first the frame of a weaving loom, then any supporting frame, such as a chassis.
From tela (cloth, canvas): a large piece of fabric such as a sheet or tarp.
From telone (a large tarp, from tela, cloth): covered with a tarp.
Not "tempestuously": tempestivamente means promptly, at the right moment, from the Latin tempestivus (timely).
Not "temporized" in the sense of stalling: temporizzati means timed, set to run on a timer, from tempo (time).
From tendere (to stretch, as in "tension"): the device that keeps something taut.
From tenere (to hold): essere tenuto a is to be held to something, that is, obliged to do it.
From tergere (to wipe, as in detergent) and cristallo (glass): the thing that wipes the glass.
From terra (earth) with the suffix -iccio: loose soil or dirt.
From tessere (to weave), like the English "textile": tessuto is woven fabric, and the English "tissue" comes from the same weaving word.
From tetto (roof) with the diminutive -uccio: the small roof, meaning the sunroof.
From titolo (title): the titolare is the person in whose name something stands, the holder of a license or document.
Sounds like "tomb": picture a small stone lid set in the road, the manhole cover.
From tornare (to turn back, return): the bend where the road turns back on itself.
From tra- (through) and forare (to bore a hole, as in "perforate"): a tunnel bored through a mountain.
From the Latin traiectus (a crossing), the same root as the English "trajectory": a tragitto is the route from one place to another.
Related to the English "train", which once meant to drag along: trainare is to tow or haul.
From the Latin trames (a path or byway): tramite means by way of or through.
From trarre (to draw out) and ne: literally take that out, so except.
From tra- (across) and correre (to run): time runs across, so it passes or elapses.
From trascurare (to neglect), built on curare (to care for): small enough to be neglected, so negligible.
From tratto (a stroke or short line): drawn in short strokes, so dashed.
From tra- and tenere (to hold): held back or restrained, like the English "retain", also built on the Latin tenere.
From trarre (to draw), like the English "tract": a stretch of road drawn from one point to another.
From traverso (crosswise), related to the English "traverse": a street that crosses the main one.
Related to the English "trumpet": a tromba is a trumpet, and also a vehicle's horn.
Related to the English "tutelage" and "tutor": all come from the Latin tueri (to watch over, protect).
From udire (to hear), related to the English "audio" and "audible".
Not "ulterior" in the sense of hidden: ulteriore means further or additional.
Not "uniquely" in the sense of remarkably: unicamente means solely or only.
Not "unique" in the sense of special: unico means the only one or single, and senso unico is a one-way street.
Sounds like "hurt": urtare is to strike or bump into, and an urto is the impact.
From the Latin urere (to burn), the same root as the English "combustion".
Related to the English legal word "usufruct": both join the Latin usus (use) and fructus (fruit, benefit).
Not "usury": in this bank usura means wear, the gradual using up of a part such as a tire.
Not "usurious": usurati means worn out, from usura (wear).
From the Latin utens (using), related to the English "utility": an utente is a user.
Related to the English "vagabond": both come from the Latin vagari (to wander).
From valere (to be worth or to hold good), related to the English "valid" and "value".
Related to valico, a mountain pass: valicare is to cross over a barrier, such as a line on the road.
From vasca (tub, basin) with the diminutive ending -etta: a small basin, here the reservoir that holds a fluid.
From vedere (to see): a vedente is a person who sees, so non vedente means blind.
Related to the English "velocipede", from the Latin velox (fast) and pes, pedis (foot): the legal word for a pedal cycle.
Not "verify": verificarsi means to occur or to happen, so si verifica un guasto means a fault occurs.
Related to the English "varnish", which comes from the same medieval word; in Italian vernice means paint in general.
From the Latin versare (to turn), from the same root as "reverse": pouring means tipping a container over. Versarvi means to pour onto it.
From the Latin vitrum (glass), the root of the English "vitreous": vetri are panes of glass, here the windows of a vehicle.
From the Latin vectura (transport), from vehere (to carry), the same root as "vehicle": a vettura is a passenger car.
From the Latin vetare (to forbid), the source of the English "veto": vietare means to forbid, and vietato means forbidden.
From the Latin vigere (to be strong, to thrive), the root of "vigor": a rule that vige is in force.
Not "vigil": as a noun, vigile means a municipal police officer, from the same Latin root as "vigilant" (watchful).
From vincolo (a bond or tie), from the Latin vinculum (chain): vincolato means bound or tied to something.
Not "viscous" (thick): viscido means slippery or slimy, as a wet or greasy surface is.
Not a "visit" in the social sense: here visita means a medical examination by a doctor.
Related to the English "visage", both from the Latin visus (sight, appearance): viso means face.
Not the adjective "visual": as a noun, visuale means the view or line of sight a driver has.
Not "visualize" in the sense of imagining: visualizzare means to make something visible or to show it clearly.
From vita (life), as in "vital": a vitalizio is an income paid for the rest of a person's life.
Not the English "viva voce" (spoken aloud): here viva voce names a hands-free speakerphone, literally "live voice".
Also the ordinary word for "flying", from volare (to fly); as a noun in a vehicle, volante is the steering wheel.
From zebra: zebrature are painted stripes like a zebra's, the hatched white markings on the road surface.
